newsitem.title: USA: U.S personal income, spending signals brisk growth.
newsitem.headline: U.S personal income, spending signals brisk growth.

text.p: A hefty 0.9 percent gain in U.S. personal income coupled with a modest 0.3 percent rise in consumption shows the economy continues to expand at a brisk pace and may still be running above trend, analysts said.

"Obviously, it's a bit of a relief to see consumption slow down from January's pace, but I think it might be premature to assume that the economy has turned the corner towards more sustainable growth," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets.
February's income gain was the largest since June 1996.

Personal income in January was revised upward to a 0.4 percent rise from a previously reported 0.3 percent increase. January's personal consumption was ratcheted up to a whopping 1.0 percent gain from a previously reported 0.7 percent rise.

"These numbers are still very consistent with strong economic activity," Low said. "And particularly with this kind of income growth, I don't think we can yet say for sure that consumer spending has slowed."
Consumer spending is one of the main engines driving the economy as it accounts for some two-thirds of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Tainer estimated that the economy could grow at about a 3.5 percent annualized pace in the first quarter of this year.
"All in all, I think these are strong numbers suggesting that consumers could still keep on spending and they certainly confirm what the (Federal Reserve) did," Tainer said.
Last Tuesday, Fed policymakers increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent, marking the first time the central bank had tightened credit in slightly more that two years.
U.S. Treasuries had registered a modest positive reaction to the personal income and spending data on Monday.
While February's income and spending report is important, analysts predicted the markets will watch more closely the flood of data due out later this week.

"Probably more important for the markets than the consumption numbers here would be tomorrow's purchasing managers numbers and certainly the payroll employment on Friday," said Larry Wipf, an economist at Norwest Corp.
After the Fed hike last week, the market is looking for the "second shoe to drop," Wipf added. "That makes the upcoming economic numbers even more important."
